a: she pressed him to ask her father for a field
p: The Hebrew says Achsah urged Othniel. The Greek and Latin say Othniel urged her. The same issue arises at Joshua 15:18.

readings.en: she urged him to ask her father for the field
readings.plain: she pressed him to ask her father for a field

readings.w: Septuagint (both A and B texts); Vulgate
readings.orig: καὶ ἐπέσειεν αὐτὴν Γοθονιηλ τοῦ αἰτῆσαι παρὰ τοῦ πατρὸς αὐτῆς ἀγρόν
readings.en: and Othniel urged her to ask her father for a field
readings.plain: Othniel pressed her to ask her father for a field

why: The Hebrew is the harder reading, since Achsah then asks herself; the Greek smooths the story so the one urged is the one who asks. The Plain English follows the Hebrew, as at Joshua 15:18.
b: In the Hebrew, Achsah persuades her husband to ask, then asks Caleb herself; readers have long noticed the gap. The Greek and Latin make Othniel the one who urges, which makes the story run smoothly. Many modern scholars prefer the Greek here; most English versions keep the Hebrew and some footnote the Greek.

a: Judah captured Gaza and its territory, Ashkelon and its territory, and Ekron and its territory
p: The Greek says Judah did not take Gaza, Ashkelon and Ekron, and adds Ashdod. It fits 1:19 and 3:3.

readings.en: And Judah captured Gaza and its territory ...
readings.plain: Judah captured Gaza and its territory, Ashkelon and its territory, and Ekron and its territory

readings.orig: καὶ οὐκ ἐκληρονόμησεν Ιουδας τὴν Γάζαν οὐδὲ τὰ ὅρια αὐτῆς ...
readings.en: And Judah did not take possession of Gaza or its territory, or Ashkelon ... or Ekron ... or Ashdod and its territories
readings.plain: But Judah did not take possession of Gaza and its territory, Ashkelon and its territory, Ekron and its territory, or Ashdod and its territory

why: The Hebrew is the received text and the harder reading, since it seems to clash with 1:19 and 3:3. The Greek looks like a correction that brings the verse into line with the rest of the book.
b: In 1:19 Judah "could not drive out" the people of the plain, and in 3:3 the five rulers of the Philistines are still there. The Greek reading removes the tension. Some scholars think the Greek is original and the Hebrew lost a negative; most think the Greek translator, or the Hebrew text he used, corrected a difficulty. The Hebrew may record a brief raid rather than lasting control.

p: The A text of the Greek has "Amorite" and "Idumean" side by side, which suits a border in the far south, toward Edom.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Septuagint, B text (Vaticanus group); Targum, Vulgate
readings.en: and the border of the Amorite
readings.plain: The border of the Amorites

readings.orig: καὶ τὸ ὅριον τοῦ Αμορραίου ὁ Ιδουμαῖος
readings.en: and the border of the Amorite, the Idumean
readings.plain: The border of the Amorites, the Edomites,

why: Every witness has "Amorite." The A text's doublet, "the Amorite, the Idumean," probably records an early correction to "Edomite" copied in beside the older word. That is evidence for an original "Edomite," the reading George Moore and Robert Boling prefer, but no manuscript has "Edomite" alone, so the Plain English keeps the Hebrew.
b: Scorpion Pass (Akrabbim) and Sela mark the southern edge of the land toward Edom (Numbers 34:3–4; Joshua 15:1–3). Since the Amorites of 1:34–35 lived far to the north-west, some scholars think "Edomites" was the original, the two words being easy to confuse in Hebrew script ('dmy and 'mry). Others keep "Amorites" as a general name for the land's earlier inhabitants.

a: from Gilgal to Bochim and said
p: The Greek adds that the angel went on "to Bethel and to the house of Israel."

readings.en: from Gilgal to Bochim and said
readings.plain: from Gilgal to Bochim and said

readings.w: Septuagint (A and B texts, with small differences)
readings.orig: ἀπὸ Γαλγαλ ἐπὶ τὸν Κλαυθμῶνα καὶ ἐπὶ Βαιθηλ καὶ ἐπὶ τὸν οἶκον Ισραηλ καὶ εἶπεν πρὸς αὐτούς
readings.en: from Gilgal to the Place of Weeping and to Bethel and to the house of Israel, and said to them
readings.plain: from Gilgal to Bochim, to Bethel and to the house of Israel, and said to them

why: The Hebrew is shorter and the Greek's additions look like explanations: Bochim was linked with Bethel, where Deborah's nurse was buried under the "oak of weeping" (Genesis 35:8).
b: Many scholars think Bochim was at or near Bethel, and the Greek makes the link plain. Bethel was where the ark stood in this period (20:26–27), which would explain why the people sacrificed there (2:5).

a: They will become barbs in your sides
p: The Hebrew is short: "they will be to you as sides." Ancient versions guessed at the missing word.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex) (understood from Numbers 33:55); Targum
readings.en: and they shall be to you as sides
readings.plain: They will become barbs in your sides

readings.en: and they will be distresses to you
readings.plain: They will become a distress to you

readings.en: so that you have enemies
readings.plain: They will become enemies to you

why: The Hebrew "as sides" is best read as shorthand for Numbers 33:55, "barbs in your sides" in the site's Plain English, which Joshua 23:13 also echoes. The other versions are attempts to make sense of a hard phrase, or may reflect a Hebrew word for "enemies" (tsarim) instead of "sides" (tsiddim).
b: The words for "sides" and "enemies" or "distress" look alike in Hebrew. Some scholars correct the text to "enemies"; most keep "sides" and supply "thorns" from Numbers.

a: I am the one who brought you up from Egypt
p: In the Hebrew the angel speaks as God. Both Greek texts make him quote God instead, in two different ways.

readings.en: I brought you up from Egypt
readings.plain: I am the one who brought you up from Egypt

readings.orig: τάδε λέγει κύριος ἀνεβίβασα ὑμᾶς ἐξ Αἰγύπτου
readings.en: Thus says the Lord: I brought you up from Egypt
readings.plain: This is what the LORD says: I am the one who brought you up from Egypt

readings.orig: κύριος κύριος ἀνεβίβασεν ὑμᾶς ἐξ Αἰγύπτου
readings.en: The Lord, the Lord brought you up from Egypt
readings.plain: The LORD, the LORD, brought you up from Egypt

why: The Hebrew is the harder reading, since an angel says "I" for God. The B text adds a prophet's formula; the A text turns God's "I" into the third person. Both look like ways of easing the same difficulty.
b: The A text also adds "to give you" after "the land I promised your ancestors with an oath." Like the Targum, which makes the speaker a prophet, the Greek treats the messenger as one who quotes God. This is the oldest evidence for the "messenger" reading discussed in the note on 2:1.

p: The Hebrew says "the LORD" turned to Gideon. Both Greek texts say "the angel of the LORD."

readings.en: and the LORD turned to him
readings.plain: The LORD

readings.en: the angel of the Lord
readings.plain: The angel of the LORD

why: The Hebrew is the harder reading: it moves from the angel to the LORD without warning. The Greek keeps the angel as the speaker, which looks like a scribe easing the shift.
b: See the note on 6:14. The Greek makes the same change in 6:16 (see the next entry) but keeps "the Lord" in 6:23.

a: The LORD answered, "I will be with you.
t: "I will be with you," or "the Lord will"
p: In the Greek the angel speaks and promises that "the Lord will be with you," keeping God and messenger apart.

readings.orig: וַיֹּאמֶר אֵלָיו יְהוָה כִּי אֶהְיֶה עִמָּךְ
readings.en: And the LORD said to him, Surely I will be with you
readings.plain: The LORD answered, "I will be with you.

readings.orig: καὶ εἶπεν πρὸς αὐτὸν ὁ ἄγγελος κυρίου κύριος ἔσται μετὰ σοῦ
readings.en: And the angel of the Lord said to him, The Lord will be with you
readings.plain: The angel of the LORD answered, "The LORD will be with you.

why: The Hebrew "I will be" (ehyeh) echoes God's words to Moses at the bush (Exodus 3:12, 14) and is the harder reading. The Greek's change of speaker and person avoids having God himself appear.

a: But if you do not go with me, I will not go.
p: The Greek adds a reason for Barak's request: he does not know the day the LORD's angel will give him success.

readings.en: but if you will not go with me, I will not go
readings.plain: But if you do not go with me, I will not go.

readings.orig: ... ὅτι οὐκ οἶδα τὴν ἡμέραν ἐν ᾗ εὐοδοῖ κύριος τὸν ἄγγελον μετ' ἐμοῦ
readings.en: ... for I do not know the day on which the Lord prospers the angel with me
readings.plain: But if you do not go with me, I will not go. For I do not know the day when the LORD will give his angel success with me.

why: The Hebrew is shorter, and the Greek addition looks like an early explanation that softens Barak's hesitation: he wants the prophet with him to know God's timing.
b: The addition makes Barak's request sound like piety rather than fear, and Deborah's reply in 4:14 ("This is the day") answers it. Some scholars think it could be original, lost from the Hebrew; most see it as an early interpretation.

a: When hair flies loose in Israel
t: Loose hair, leaders, or a revelation?
p: A hard opening line. The two Greek text forms read it two different ways.

readings.en: when locks are let loose in Israel
readings.plain: When hair flies loose in Israel

readings.w: Septuagint, A text (Codex Alexandrinus and related manuscripts)
readings.orig: ἐν τῷ ἄρξασθαι ἀρχηγοὺς ἐν Ισραηλ
readings.en: when leaders began to lead in Israel
readings.plain: When leaders took the lead in Israel

readings.w: Septuagint, B text (Codex Vaticanus and related manuscripts)
readings.en: a revelation was revealed in Israel
readings.plain: A revelation was revealed in Israel

why: The Hebrew pera'ot most likely means long, loose hair, worn by warriors under a vow (compare Numbers 6:5; Deuteronomy 32:42). The A text took the root as "lead," the B text as "uncover." Both are early guesses at a rare word.
b: Rahlfs prints the whole book in both forms; here they differ in meaning. Many English versions follow the A-type sense ("when the leaders took the lead"); others keep the hair.

a: And when the Israelites cried out to the LORD over what Midian was doing,
p: 4QJudg-a skips 6:7–10, the prophet's speech. These four entries go together.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Septuagint, Targum, Vulgate
readings.en: (the verse as printed)
readings.plain: And when the Israelites cried out to the LORD over what Midian was doing,

readings.en: (lacking; the scroll runs from 6:6 to 6:11)

why: Every other witness has these verses, and the scroll is a small fragment. The Plain English keeps them, while noting the scroll's testimony.
b: 4QJudg-a, a Dead Sea Scroll fragment from the first century BC, has 6:2–6 followed directly by 6:11. Julio Trebolle Barrera, who published it, argued that it preserves an older form of the book, before an editor added the prophet's speech. Others think a scribe skipped the passage, by accident or on purpose, or that the fragment is an excerpt. Scholars had already noticed that 6:7–10 reads like an editorial insertion: it interrupts the story, and its sermon resembles 2:1–5 and 10:11–14. If Trebolle is right, the scroll is rare manuscript evidence of how the book was edited.

a: the LORD sent a prophet to the Israelites. He said to them, "This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: I brought you up from Egypt. I brought you out of the house of slaves.
p: 4QJudg-a skips 6:7–10, the prophet's speech. These four entries go together.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Septuagint, Targum, Vulgate
readings.en: (the verse as printed)
readings.plain: the LORD sent a prophet to the Israelites. He said to them, "This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: I brought you up from Egypt. I brought you out of the house of slaves.

readings.en: (lacking; the scroll runs from 6:6 to 6:11)

why: Every other witness has these verses, and the scroll is a small fragment. The Plain English keeps them, while noting the scroll's testimony.
b: See the entry at 6:7. The scroll fragment goes straight from Midian's raids (6:6) to the angel under the oak (6:11).

a: I rescued you from the power of Egypt and from the power of all who oppressed you. I drove them out ahead of you and gave you their land.
p: 4QJudg-a skips 6:7–10, the prophet's speech. These four entries go together.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Septuagint, Targum, Vulgate
readings.en: (the verse as printed)
readings.plain: I rescued you from the power of Egypt and from the power of all who oppressed you. I drove them out ahead of you and gave you their land.

readings.en: (lacking; the scroll runs from 6:6 to 6:11)

why: Every other witness has these verses, and the scroll is a small fragment. The Plain English keeps them, while noting the scroll's testimony.
b: See the entry at 6:7. The scroll fragment goes straight from Midian's raids (6:6) to the angel under the oak (6:11).

a: I told you, 'I am the LORD your God. Do not fear the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you are living.' But you have not listened to my voice."
p: 4QJudg-a skips 6:7–10, the prophet's speech. These four entries go together.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Septuagint, Targum, Vulgate
readings.en: (the verse as printed)
readings.plain: I told you, 'I am the LORD your God. Do not fear the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you are living.' But you have not listened to my voice."

readings.en: (lacking; the scroll runs from 6:6 to 6:11)

why: Every other witness has these verses, and the scroll is a small fragment. The Plain English keeps them, while noting the scroll's testimony.
b: See the entry at 6:7. The scroll fragment goes straight from Midian's raids (6:6) to the angel under the oak (6:11).

a: he made the men of Succoth learn
p: The Hebrew says Gideon "made them know"; the Greek says he "threshed" them, as he had threatened in 8:7.

readings.en: and he made the men of Succoth know by them
readings.plain: he made the men of Succoth learn

readings.w: Septuagint (A and B texts), Vulgate, Syriac
readings.orig: καὶ ἠλόησεν ἐν αὐτοῖς τοὺς ἄνδρας Σοκχωθ
readings.en: and he threshed the men of Succoth with them
readings.plain: he threshed the men of Succoth

why: The Hebrew makes sense as it stands and is the harder reading. The Greek matches the threat of 8:7 and probably reads a Hebrew word that differs by one letter (vayyadosh, "threshed").
b: Many scholars prefer the Greek, since it fulfills 8:7 word for word, and yada' and dush are easily confused. The Plain English keeps the Hebrew but the note at 8:7 explains the threshing.

a: Then I would remove Abimelech." And he said to Abimelech, "Make your army big and come out!"
t: A challenge sent, or only boasted?
p: The Hebrew says Gaal spoke to Abimelech, who was not there. The Greek keeps it in Gaal's boast: "I would say to Abimelech."

readings.orig: וְאָסִירָה אֶת־אֲבִימֶלֶךְ וַיֹּאמֶר לַאֲבִימֶלֶךְ רַבֶּה צְבָאֲךָ וָצֵאָה
readings.en: and I would remove Abimelech. And he said to Abimelech, Increase your army and come out
readings.plain: Then I would remove Abimelech." And he said to Abimelech, "Make your army big and come out!"

readings.orig: καὶ μεταστήσω τὸν Αβιμελεχ καὶ ἐρῶ τῷ Αβιμελεχ Πλήθυνον τὴν δύναμίν σου καὶ ἔξελθε
readings.en: and I would remove Abimelech, and I would say to Abimelech, Increase your power and come out
readings.plain: Then I would remove Abimelech. I would say to Abimelech, 'Make your army big and come out!'"

why: The Hebrew may mean Gaal shouted a challenge to the absent Abimelech, a drunken taunt, or sent it by word of mouth. The Greek reads one letter differently and makes it part of the boast. The Plain English keeps the Hebrew.
b: The Hebrew vayyomer, "and he said," differs from ve'omar, "and I would say," by a small change in the consonants. Many translations follow the Greek here. Either way, the speech is bluster at a feast, and Zebul passes it on (9:31).

p: The Greek reads "Midian," the enemy of Gideon's story. The Hebrew "Maon" names a people not mentioned elsewhere in the book.

readings.en: and Maon
readings.plain: Maon

readings.en: Midian
readings.plain: Midian

why: The Hebrew is the harder reading, since no oppression by Maon is told. "Midian" in the Greek looks like a correction to match chapters 6–8, though it could be original. Both Greek texts read Midian here, in a different order (A: Sidonians, Midian, Amalek; B: Sidonians, Amalek, Midian).
b: See the note on "Maon." Several modern versions follow the Greek here and footnote the Hebrew.

a: in one of the towns of Gilead
p: The Hebrew says "in the towns of Gilead." The Greek says "in his town, Gilead," which most translations follow in sense.

readings.en: in the towns of Gilead
readings.plain: in one of the towns of Gilead

readings.en: in his town, Gilead
readings.plain: in his town, in Gilead

why: The Hebrew plural is odd but is the harder reading. The Plain English keeps it, with "one of" to make sense, as many versions do. The Greek reflects a Hebrew text that read "in his town" (be'iro).
b: See the note on this phrase for the midrash that took the plural literally.
